title: What prayer is (CCC 2559–2565)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the tenth commandment, and the end of Part Three: envy, greed, and poverty of heart. Your line was enough. Whose good news did you manage to be glad about? Now, Part Four. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-seven.

A well in Samaria, outside a town, and a stranger sitting on its edge, tired from walking. A woman comes out with her jar, around the sixth hour, the Gospel says. And the stranger speaks first. Not with a sermon. With a request. "Give me to drink." Near the start of its fourth part, on prayer, the Catechism goes to that well. Before it says anything about how to pray, it wants you to notice who asked first. Today: what prayer is.
screen: `A WELL IN SAMARIA.` → `A WOMAN WITH A JAR.` → `GIVE ME TO DRINK.`

segments.voice: The Catechism gives three words for prayer: gift, covenant, communion. First, gift. It quotes Saint Thérèse of Lisieux, who described prayer as a surge of the heart, a simple look turned toward heaven, a cry of thanks and of love in trial as in joy. And it quotes Saint John Damascene: prayer is the raising of one's mind and heart to God. Then it says something humbling. We don't know how to pray as we ought. Humility is where prayer begins. Which brings it to the well. In John's Gospel Jesus tells the woman, "If thou didst know the gift of God," she would have asked him, and he would have given her living water. The Catechism reads the scene this way: it is Jesus who is thirsty, and his asking comes from the depth of God's desire for us. Then it borrows a line from Saint Augustine: God thirsts that we may thirst for him. Whether we know it or not, prayer is the meeting of two thirsts. Second, covenant. The Catechism says prayer comes from the heart, the hidden center of a person, the place of decision, the place of truth, where we choose life or death. And prayer is covenant because it's a relationship God started, binding him and us together in Christ. Third, communion. In the New Covenant, the Catechism says, prayer is the living relationship of God's children with their Father, with his Son Jesus Christ, and with the Holy Spirit. Not a technique. A life with someone. So before a single instruction, the Catechism says: you're not the one who started this. The thirst came looking for you.
screen: `PRAYER IS A GIFT.` · `GIVE ME TO DRINK.` · `PRAYER IS A COVENANT.` · `PRAYER IS COMMUNION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: receive prayer as a gift. Settle, and breathe. Don't try to say anything yet. Picture the well, the heat, the jar, and the stranger who asks first. Let the idea sit that the asking might come from the other side. Notice your own thirst, whatever it's for today: rest, peace, someone to listen. If you pray, you can simply turn toward God, the way Thérèse put it, a simple look. If you don't, just stay with the thirst, without fixing it. The bell holds the time.
What prayer is. In Catholic teaching, a gift, a covenant and a communion: the raising of mind and heart to God, who comes looking for us first. Today's word.
Your line: god thirsts that we thirst. Today, the next time you're thirsty, before you drink, remember the well, and who asked first. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-seven.

howItsDone: Catholics pray in many ways, alone and together, aloud and in silence; the Catechism opens its teaching on prayer by calling it a gift from God, a covenant relationship and a communion with the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.
